body.text: As James Bond, Robert Pattinson prepares to lead his biggest franchise yet
Who knew Twilight would have predicted the next 007?
Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond, succeeding fellow Englishman Daniel Craig in one of Hollywood's most recognisable roles.
But it's a scene from Pattinson's breakout film that has resurfaced for its eerily prophetic nature.
In the 2008 vampire hit, the prom theme is Monte Carlo, with the students of Forks High School told to think "gambling, tuxedos and Bond … James Bond".
The camera than cuts to Pattinson's Edward Cullen, who steps out of a sleek silver Volvo sporting Ray-Bans and a smirk.
Fast forward nearly 20 years and that parallel is now a reality.
New era for 007
Pattinson brings maximum star power to the James Bond role, reportedly beating out fellow Brits Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O'Connor.

"I think Robert Pattinson is one of the most dynamic and most interesting actors working in Hollywood," film critic Luke Goodsell says, noting his roles in this year's Primetime, The Drama and The Odyssey.
Pattinson's appointment also marks the first time James Bond has been cast since Amazon reportedly paid more than $1 billion for the 007 intellectual property in February last year.
"It's been remarked on that it's the first time the Bond franchise has cast a big A-Lister," Goodsell says.
"Obviously, Roger Moore was famous for The Saint and Pierce Brosnan was famous to some degree for Remington Steele, but this is the first time they've really gone for an A-list actor.
Which is unusual, Goodsell says, because "the former producer Barbara Broccoli was always adamant that the actor should not be bigger than 007".
"But I think repeating the same old playbook where they cast a relative unknown would be the least interesting choice at this point in the franchise," Goodsell says.
"For them to dive straight in, headlong into a major movie star, and a really interesting and slippery actor who is also a movie star, is a really fascinating choice."
Wizards, vampires and Batman
Pattinson is no stranger to franchises.

One of his first major roles was in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005, where he played the dashing but doomed Cedric Diggory, his death marking the moment the series goes from whimsical to something much darker.

But Pattinson was launched to stratospheric levels of fame in 2008 when he landed the role of Edward Cullen in Twilight, the film's success cementing his heart-throb status in Hollywood and making him a household name, in the homes of teenage girls, at least.

Despite his fame, Pattinson rallied against his handsome, alluring on-screen persona, instead using his countless interviews on the Twilight press junket to begin a years-long affinity for creating bizarre, fabricated stories.
In a 2024 interview with The New York Times, the actor revisited a 2011 interview in which he spoke extensively about watching a clown die in a little-car explosion as a kid.
"There was absolutely no hesitation at all [in my voice]," Pattinson said with a combination of "pride and alarm".
His reason? Boredom, explaining "the only thing people would ever ask me about was being famous" and "you go into, like, a fugue state".
Goodsell says Pattinson's career has been "compelling to watch".

Post Twilight, Goodsell says Pattinson and his co-star Kristen Stewart were "assumed, I think, to be doomed after that, and both of them went out and said, 'OK, we're going to revive our careers in different ways'".
With five Twilight movies complete, Pattinson had the freedom to get weird.
He dived into independent films, teaming up with David Cronenberg for Cosmopolis, starring in the Safdie brothers' Good Time, and Robert Eggers' psychological horror The Lighthouse.
In 2020, he would star in one his most Bond-esque roles to date: Christopher Nolan's Tenet.
He even explored voice acting for the English dub of Hayao Miyazaki's The Boy and the Heron.
"He really kind of, let's just say it, lets his freak flag fly. He loves a weird voice," Goodsell says.

"One of my favourite bits of Pattinson lore is his great lying streak in interviews and I think in any other profession, that might be a problem, but for an actor, I think it's an exceptional skill and I think you can see him kind of relishing each of his roles that he's done."
Bond for the digital age
One of Pattinson's biggest roles in recent years has been playing Batman, begging the question: can you be both Bruce Wayne and James Bond?
Scheduling wise, yes.
The Batman Part II has been delayed until 2028 for a variety of reasons, including industry strikes and director Matt Reeves stepping away for personal reasons.
"It's weird, a lot of people are saying, 'oh, well, you can't be the Batman and be James Bond'", Goodsell says.

"But I feel like — even though his Batman is great and it was hugely popular — I guess we could say the mark of Pattinson's talent as an actor is he hasn't been defined by the Batman. He hasn't been defined by Edward Cullen."
In Goodsell's view, "the great thing about Pattinson is he's so unpredictable".
"He can play very serious and very grim. And he can also play very funny, and he's also got a very eccentric streak in him," Goodsell says.
"I think that's what's most exciting about him playing Bond because he might do something really out of the box with that role.
"I guess the cliche might be every era gets the Bond they deserve or the Bond that suits the time and I think Robert Pattinson is an actor that suits this era.
"He's a Bond for the digital age."
